title: Getting dressed in two languages: four clothing words and one question
description: Mornings already follow a script: shirt, socks, shoes, coat. Say those four words in the language you are building every day and let your child choose between two options.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: Getting dressed in two languages: four clothing words and one question
body:
Mornings are already a script. The same things go on in roughly the same order every day, which is exactly what new words need: the same words, in context, every day, without setting aside any extra time.

Start with four items your child puts on most mornings: shirt, socks, shoes, coat. In Spanish: la camisa, los calcetines, los zapatos, el abrigo. Four is enough. Mornings are rushed, and a routine that makes you late will not last the week.

The routine has one phrase and one question.

The phrase is "put on your…". If you are building Spanish: "Ponte los zapatos." If you are building English: "put on your shoes." Use the language you are building for those four items only — the rest of the morning can run in whatever language you normally use.

The question is a choice between two. Hold up two shirts: "¿Esta o esta?" — or "this one or this one?". Better still, name the colours: "¿La camisa roja o la azul?" / "the red shirt or the blue one?". A choice makes your child say a word to get something they want, which is different from repeating after you.

Then hand the job over. After a few days, ask your child what comes next and let them announce it: "¡los calcetines!" or "socks!". Children like being the one who knows the order.

When a morning goes wrong — and some will — drop the game for the day. Getting out of the door matters more. The routine will still be there tomorrow, and that is its whole strength.

After a week or two, add one item at a time as the season calls for it: hat, gloves, scarf — el gorro, los guantes, la bufanda. Keep the original four; they are the anchor.

One small detail worth keeping from the start: in Spanish the colour comes after the noun and matches it — la camisa roja, los zapatos rojos. There is no need to explain this to a child. Say it that way every time and the pattern is there to be heard.
qa_checklist: A bilingual (EN/ES) reader checks both languages, not a tool
No claims about fluency, test scores or developmental outcomes
Every activity works with what is already in the house: no printer, no purchase
Original text written for this page, not lifted from the book
CTA is honest: a Kindle vocabulary book read on a screen, lists copied into a notebook
semantic_review: English body; Spanish clothing nouns chosen for wide intelligibility (la camisa, los calcetines, los zapatos, el abrigo). 'Ponte los zapatos' / 'put on your shoes' and the colour choice given in both directions. Word for pants/trousers avoided because it differs between English variants.
claims_check: No outcome promises. The text says what to do and how long it takes; it does not claim fluency, school results or cognitive benefits.

checks_run: direction symmetry (either language may be the target)
resolved: examples run in both directions and the instructions name 'the language you are building'
Spanish kept to short words and phrases with articles and accents checked
closing mention of the book cut to one sentence after the activity is fully explained
avoided clothing words with strong regional variants (T-shirt, jacket, sweater; pants/trousers in English)
demonstratives written without accent (esta), per current RAE spelling
adjective agreement shown by example only (la camisa roja, los zapatos rojos)
closing sentence about the book removed: the CTA lives on the book card (CLAUDE.md, 12 Sep round four)
